lead: Riverside is hot and dry most of the year, so its water damage starts inside: slab leaks, water heaters and aging pipes. Rare heavy storms add flash flooding.
risk: slab leaks, water heater failures and flash floods
risk_short: slab leaks, water heaters, flash floods
why: More than half of Riverside homes were built before 1980, many on concrete slabs with copper pipe run underneath. Hard water and decades of use wear those lines thin. A pinhole leak under the slab can run for weeks before it shows up as a warm floor or a wet spot in the carpet. Water heaters in garages and closets fail too, and a burst tank can flood several rooms at once.

Rain is rare, but when it comes it can be heavy. In August 2023, Tropical Storm Hilary brought rare summer flooding to Southern California, including parts of the Inland Empire. Hillside streets and dry washes fill fast in storms like that. Riverside also has some mobile home parks, where leaks under the floor can go unseen. Dry air helps things dry, but hidden water still causes mold.
image_alt: Exposed old pipes on a wall during repairs
image_caption: In Riverside, hidden slab and wall leaks cause more water damage than rain.
problems: Pre-1980 homes in Magnolia Center, Arlington
Kitchens and baths in older homes
tips: Check your meter with every tap off to spot a hidden leak.
Replace a water heater that is 10 to 12 years old.
Clear yard drains before the rainy season.
Feel for warm spots on floors; they can point to a slab leak.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, the Wood Streets, Canyon Crest, Arlington, La Sierra, Magnolia Center, Orangecrest and Mission Grove, plus Corona, Moreno Valley and Jurupa Valley.

faq.q: How do I know if my Riverside home has a slab leak?
faq.a: Common signs are a warm spot on the floor, the sound of running water with taps off, a damp carpet edge and a water bill that jumps. A plumber can confirm it with pressure or sound tests. DryFlare then dries the floor and walls so mold does not set in.
